faq.question: Is Originality.ai free?
faq.answer: No. Unlike consumer detectors, Originality.ai targets publishers and agencies, so it is paid from the first scan. You can choose pay-as-you-go credit packs or a monthly subscription; heavy teams usually land on the subscription because credits burn quickly on long documents.

faq.question: Can it detect which AI model wrote a text?
faq.answer: It reports a probability score plus a breakdown of the AI models it believes contributed to the text. Treat the model attribution as a signal, not a verdict - mixed human-AI editing always lowers confidence on both sides.

faq.question: Who actually uses it?
faq.answer: Content agencies, affiliate publishers and editorial teams that buy or produce large volumes of articles. The typical workflow is: scan every submission, share the report link with the writer, and hold payment until the score clears the house threshold.

faq.question: How is it different from GPTZero?
faq.answer: GPTZero grew out of education and focuses on classroom use cases. Originality.ai grew out of content marketing and adds the commercial layer: plagiarism, fact-checking, team seats and an API. Writers get flagged by both; publishers almost always pick Originality.ai first.

pricing_details: Two payment models: pay-as-you-go credit packs (one-time purchase, credits roughly 1 credit per 100 words scanned) and monthly subscriptions starting around $14.95/mo that bundle recurring credits with team features. Plagiarism and AI detection consume credits together on combined scans. Verify current tiers on the official pricing page - detector vendors reprice often.
content:
## What Originality.ai Is, And Who It Was Built For

Most AI detectors you have heard of were built for teachers. Originality.ai was built for the people paying the invoices on the other side of that transaction: publishers, niche-site owners and content agencies that buy hundreds of articles a month and need to know - before payment, not after ranking - whether a piece is machine-generated, plagiarised, or stitched together with fabricated facts.

That difference in customer decides everything about the product. Where GPTZero optimizes for a teacher checking one essay, Originality.ai optimizes for a managing editor checking fifty submissions before Friday payroll. That means team seats, shared scan history, report links you can send to a writer, and - the feature everyone underestimates - a fact-checking assistant that flags claims in the text that look unverifiable.

## The Three Checks That Matter

A combined scan runs three engines at once. The AI detection layer scores the probability that the text was machine-generated, with a model attribution breakdown. The plagiarism layer returns matched sources with URLs, which matters because the most common fraud in content buying is not pure AI output - it is AI output lightly paraphrased from an existing article. The fact-checking layer is the newest and the most interesting: it highlights specific claims that it cannot corroborate, which catches the classic failure mode of AI-written reviews, invented statistics and nonexistent sources.

For a one-person site this can feel like overkill. For anyone who has ever paid $2,000 for a batch of forty articles and later watched a competitor copy them word-for-word, it feels like insurance.

## The Honest Limitations

Every AI detector shares the same physics: a confident human-edited AI draft can score low, and an idiosyncratic human writer can score high. Originality.ai deserves credit for publishing benchmark data and telling you which model generations it was tuned on, but no number from any detector should ever be the sole basis for firing a writer. The professional pattern is to treat the score as a conversation starter - ask the writer for drafts, docs history, or a short live-writing session - and use the detection report as evidence, not verdict.

Also budget for credits. Long documents plus combined scans burn through packs faster than the pricing page suggests. Teams scanning 100+ articles a month almost always switch to the subscription.

## How It Fits Into A Buying Workflow

The mature setup looks like this: a writer submits via Google Doc, the editor runs the Chrome extension scan without leaving the doc, the combined score is attached to the invoice, and the fact-check flags become the revision brief. Agencies that adopt this loop report fewer disputes, because the writer sees the same report the editor sees. It turns quality control from an accusation into a shared checklist.

If you are evaluating this space more broadly, our review of [GPTZero](/tools/gptzero/) covers the education-first alternative, and if your problem is rewriting flagged text rather than detecting it, [QuillBot](/tools/quillbot/) is the paraphrasing side of that workflow. For the generation side of the same pipeline, [ChatGPT](/tools/chatgpt/) and [Claude](/tools/claude/) remain the two main sources of the drafts you will be scanning.

description: One of the most-used free web AI detectors: paste text, get an instant AI-percentage score. Zero-friction for quick checks, with paid tiers for longer documents, PDF support and batch scanning.

Free tier covers most quick personal checks

faq.question: Is ZeroGPT actually free?
faq.answer: The web scanner is free for texts under the word limit, supported by ads. Longer documents, PDF batches, API access and higher daily volumes sit behind paid plans. For a one-off check of an email or essay, most people never need to pay.

faq.question: How accurate is it?
faq.answer: Honestly: treat it as a smoke detector, not a judge. Independent tests of consumer detectors - ZeroGPT included - repeatedly show false positives on human text and false negatives on heavily edited AI text. Use it for a fast first read, never as sole evidence for an accusation.

faq.question: Why is it so popular if accuracy is contested?
faq.answer: Because the friction is near zero. No account, no install, instant percentage. For 'is this paragraph AI-written?' curiosity checks, convenience beats precision - the same reason free plagiarism checkers still get massive traffic alongside enterprise tools.

faq.question: What should professionals use instead?
faq.answer: If your decisions have consequences - payroll, grades, publish/reject calls - use a workflow tool with reports and history. Our reviews of [Originality.ai](/tools/originality-ai/) and [GPTZero](/tools/gptzero/) cover the two mainstream professional options.

pricing_details: Free web scanning with per-check word limits and ads. Paid subscriptions unlock longer documents, batch processing, PDF reports, higher daily limits and API access; exact tier pricing changes frequently, so check the official pricing page. As of late 2026 expect entry paid tiers in the low tens of dollars per month.
content:
## The Detector Everyone Has Already Used

ZeroGPT is the tool behind half the 'AI percentage' screenshots you have seen on social media. Paste a paragraph, watch a progress bar, get a number - 'your text is 87% AI generated' - with suspected sentences highlighted. That loop takes under ten seconds and requires no account, which explains both its enormous popularity and its polarizing reputation.

It occupies a specific slot in the detector ecosystem: the free, instant, curiosity-tier checker. Teachers use it for quick spot checks. Students use it to pre-check assignments. Editors use it to triage a suspicious paragraph before escalating to a paid tool. Its business model is exactly what you would expect: the free scanner is the marketing, and the paid plans - longer texts, batch scans, PDF reports, API - are where professionals land after hitting word limits.

## Reading The Score Correctly

The percentage ZeroGPT shows is a probability estimate, and the marketing around consumer detectors routinely outruns the science. The failure modes are well documented across this whole category: heavily edited AI text scores human, formulaic human text (legal boilerplate, template emails, ESL academic writing) scores AI, and paraphrasing tools deliberately attack exactly the statistics detectors rely on. So the sane way to use ZeroGPT is: 0-20% probably human, 80-100% worth a closer look, anything between is noise that requires human judgment.

If the stakes are real - a hiring decision, a contract dispute, an academic misconduct case - a single free scan is not evidence. Chain it: run the same text through a second detector, look at revision history, and ask the author to walk you through their process. Our [GPTZero](/tools/gptzero/) review covers the education-focused professional option, and [Originality.ai](/tools/originality-ai/) covers the publishing-first option with plagiarism and fact-checking built in.

## Where It Fits In 2026

Two years into the AI-detection boom, the category has split into consumer instant-checkers like ZeroGPT and workflow platforms built for teams. ZeroGPT keeps winning the top of the funnel because 'paste and see' will always be the first instinct. The paid tiers are its attempt to convert that traffic into professional usage, but that is also where its thinness shows: no team seats, no scan history worth the name, no reporting layer. It is a checker, not a system.

For writers on the other side of the equation - text that keeps getting flagged - the honest fix is not a counter-detector but editing depth: adding first-hand specifics, restructuring sentences, and cutting the uniform rhythm detectors key on. If your flagged text came out of [ChatGPT](/tools/chatgpt/) or [Claude](/tools/claude/), a human editing pass usually resolves it; if you need help paraphrasing deliberately, [QuillBot](/tools/quillbot/) is the standard tool for that job.

faq.question: Who is Copyleaks for?
faq.answer: Schools, universities and companies running originality programs at scale. The LMS integrations are the giveaway: if your institution runs assignments through Canvas or Moodle, Copyleaks plugs directly into the grading flow, which consumer tools cannot do.

faq.question: Does it really detect plagiarized source code?
faq.answer: Yes - this is its most distinctive feature. It compares code structure and logic rather than just strings, which matters for computer-science courses and for companies auditing contractor-delivered codebases. Few competitors even attempt this.

faq.question: How is it priced versus GPTZero or Originality.ai?
faq.answer: Copyleaks sells page-based credits on subscriptions, with institutional and business tiers quoted on contact. For individual writers it feels pricier and more bureaucratic; for institutions with hundreds of students it usually prices better than per-seat tools.

faq.question: Can it handle non-English text?
faq.answer: That is one of its strongest cards - AI detection and plagiarism across 30+ languages, which matters for international universities and multilingual content teams. Most consumer detectors are effectively English-first.

pricing_details: Free trial scans to test the interface; paid plans are page-credit based, with individual tiers starting around $10/mo (billed annually) and institutional/business pricing quoted per volume. LMS integration and API availability vary by tier. Confirm current numbers on the official pricing page.
content:
## The Institutional Contender

If GPTZero is the classroom detector and Originality.ai is the publishing detector, Copyleaks is the one your university IT department already evaluated. It has been in the originality business longer than the AI-detection wave - it built its name on plagiarism checking for education - and it added AI content detection as the category exploded. That heritage shows in the product: where consumer tools optimize for a single paste-and-scan, Copyleaks optimizes for thousands of submissions flowing through institutional systems every semester.

The integration list is the moat. Canvas, Moodle and Blackboard plugins mean a teacher never leaves the grading flow. Google Docs and Office add-ons mean a corporate reviewer never leaves the document. For institutions, there is repository cross-comparison - every new submission is checked against everything previously scanned by the same account, which is how you catch the assignment-copied-from-last-semester problem that pure AI detectors miss entirely.

## Two Capabilities Competitors Lack

The first is source-code plagiarism detection. Copyleaks compares code semantically - structure and logic, not just text lines - which makes it the default pick for computer-science departments and for companies auditing outsourced code. No consumer AI detector offers anything equivalent.

The second is serious multilingual coverage: AI detection across 30+ languages rather than English-with-asterisks. International universities and multilingual content agencies are underserved by English-first tools, and this is quietly a deciding factor in procurement decisions.

## The Trade-Offs

The credit system is page-based rather than word-based, which constantly surprises people arriving from GPTZero or ZeroGPT - a 'page' is roughly 250 words, so long documents consume credits faster than you might model. The interface is built for administrators, not casual users; if you want a ten-second check, this is the wrong tool. And the accuracy caveat that applies to every detector applies here too: heavily edited AI text and template-driven human text both degrade scores, so institutional policies should treat detection reports as one input among several, never as automated verdicts.

For a fuller picture of the category, compare with our reviews of [GPTZero](/tools/gptzero/), [Originality.ai](/tools/originality-ai/) and the free-tier staple [ZeroGPT](/tools/zerogpt/). On the generation side of the arms race, [ChatGPT](/tools/chatgpt/) and [Claude](/tools/claude/) remain the dominant sources of the text being checked.

faq.question: What exactly is 'nano banana'?
faq.answer: An internal Google codename for its Gemini image model that escaped into the wild and went viral in mid-2026, largely on edits where a person's face stays perfectly consistent across wild scene changes. Google has since embraced the nickname. The same capability is offered through the Gemini app and the Gemini API.

faq.question: Is it free to use?
faq.answer: Yes, inside the Gemini app, within normal free-tier usage limits. Developers calling it through the Gemini API pay per generated image - roughly four cents per image at the standard tier - which is why startups building on it watch their image budgets closely.

faq.question: How does it compare with Midjourney or FLUX?
faq.answer: Different jobs. Nano Banana wins on editing and consistency - keeping the same character across a twenty-image story set. [Midjourney](/tools/midjourney/) still leads on pure aesthetic quality for finished art. If your work is product photography consistency or 'put this exact person in ten scenes', nano banana is currently the path of least resistance.

faq.question: Can it make a consistent character for a story or product line?
faq.answer: That is precisely its viral use case: upload one reference photo, then request scene changes conversationally while the identity holds. Creators use it for consistent mascots, product mockups across backgrounds, and storyboard sequences without retraining anything.

pricing_details: Free usage inside the Gemini app within daily limits; Google AI Pro/Ultra subscriptions raise limits and unlock higher-output tiers. Gemini API access is billed per image, on the order of $0.04 per generated image at the standard tier, with batch and higher-quality tiers priced separately. Check Google's current AI pricing page for exact figures.
content:
## How A Codename Became A Product Category

'Nano banana' started as Google's internal codename for the image model inside Gemini. It leaked, the AI community adopted it as an affectionate meme, and by mid-2026 the nickname had more search volume than the official product name - a genuinely rare case of a codename becoming the de facto brand. Google eventually leaned in. Today, searching 'nano banana' lands you on Gemini's image generation, and that is the product this page covers.

The capability that made it explode is specific: character-consistent editing. Upload a photo of yourself, your pet, or your product, then ask in plain language for changes - 'put this person in a Tokyo alley at night, same jacket, same face' - and the model delivers while keeping identity intact. Previous image tools treated every edit as a fresh roll of the dice; nano banana treats your reference as an anchor.

## Why Creators Picked It Up So Fast

The consistency unlock turns five workflows from painful to trivial. Storyboard sequences with the same protagonist across ten scenes. Product mockups where the item stays identical across backgrounds. Personal-brand imagery that actually looks like you. Mascot-driven content series where the character must survive image after image. Before nano banana, each of these needed LoRA training or painstaking manual compositing; now it is a conversation with the Gemini app - free at the basic tier.

The conversational editing model is the second half of the appeal. There are no masks, no layers, no selection tools. You describe the change, inspect the result, and refine by talking. It feels less like Photoshop and more like art direction.

## Where It Does Not Win

For finished, gallery-grade aesthetics, [Midjourney](/tools/midjourney/) remains the connoisseur's pick - its default output has a finished quality nano banana does not consistently match. For maximum control over composition and professional print resolution, dedicated tools still lead. And Google's content filters are stricter than specialist image platforms, which matters if your use case brushes up against edgy territory.

For developers, the real story is the API: the same model is callable from the Gemini API at roughly four cents an image, which has made it the default image engine for a wave of small apps and agents. Combined with text and vision in the same [Gemini](/tools/gemini/) family, it lets a single API key cover a full multimodal pipeline.

## Practical Tips

Reference quality is everything - a clean, well-lit source photo produces dramatically better consistent edits than a blurry one. Iterate conversationally rather than re-describing from scratch; the model remembers the thread. And for multi-image character sets, generate the anchor image first, then derive variations from it instead of starting fresh each time. If your pipeline also needs video from stills, [Veo](/tools/veo/) is Google's motion-side counterpart, and for pure text generation around your images, [ChatGPT](/tools/chatgpt/) and [Claude](/tools/claude/) cover the copy layer.

faq.question: Who makes Hailuo AI?
faq.answer: MiniMax, the Chinese AI company behind the MiniMax language models. Hailuo is their video generation product family, and it has become one of the most competitive entries in the text-to-video race alongside [Kling](/tools/kling-ai/), [Runway](/tools/runway/) and [Veo](/tools/veo/).

faq.question: Is Hailuo AI free to use?
faq.answer: The web and mobile apps allocate free credits daily, enough for a handful of standard-quality generations per day. Paid subscriptions buy HD resolution, longer clips, faster queue priority and larger monthly volumes - the standard freemium pattern for Chinese video models.

faq.question: What is it best at?
faq.answer: Human motion. Early AI video's tell was the uncanny walk - melting limbs, sliding feet. Hailuo's motion synthesis handles people walking, dancing and interacting with objects more naturally than most rivals, which is why short-form creators use it for character-driven clips.

faq.question: How does it compare with Kling or Veo?
faq.answer: Kling competes hard on duration and physics realism, Veo on cinematic quality and Google-stack integration, Hailuo on motion fluidity and free-tier generosity. Many creators keep two or three subscriptions and route each shot to whichever model fits the scene.

pricing_details: Free daily credits on web and mobile. Paid subscription tiers (names and prices revise frequently) add HD output, longer clip durations, priority queueing and commercial usage rights at volumes suited to short-form creators and small studios. Check the official pricing page for current tiers.
content:
## The Motion Specialist Of The Video Race

The AI video race of 2025-2026 has four names that matter: [Runway](/tools/runway/) with its head start and professional tooling, [Veo](/tools/veo/) with Google's cinematic polish, [Kling](/tools/kling-ai/) with its duration and physics push, and Hailuo AI - MiniMax's entry - with a specific superpower: the most natural human motion in the consumer tier.

That superpower sounds narrow until you watch the failures it fixes. First-generation AI video had a tell you could spot in one second: people walking like their joints were borrowed from a slideshow. Hailuo's models handle gait, dance, sports and hand-object interaction with a fluidity that passes casual viewing, which unlocked the use case that dominates short-form content today - character-driven clips for TikTok, Reels and Shorts.

## The Creator Economics

Hailuo's second strategic weapon is its free tier. Daily free credits mean a creator can prototype shots every single day without a subscription - a sharp contrast with the trial-gated Western tools. The standard loop looks like this: draft the shot with free credits, iterate prompts on the strongest candidate, then upgrade that one shot to HD through a paid tier if it makes the final cut. For solo creators and small teams, this pay-for-the-keepers model keeps costs near zero until something actually ships.

Image-to-video is the other heavily used mode. Feed it a character still - increasingly generated with consistent identity by models like [nano-banana](/tools/nano-banana/) - and Hailuo animates it while preserving likeness, with camera-movement controls for pans, dollies and follow shots. The still-to-motion pipeline has quietly become the standard workflow for AI-assisted short drama and product teaser content.

## The Honest Gaps

Clip length caps trail the competition - if your format needs long continuous takes, [Kling](/tools/kling-ai/) currently pushes further. Audio generation is thinner than the video core, so voiceovers and music usually come from dedicated tools like [ElevenLabs](/tools/elevenlabs/) and [Suno](/tools/suno/). And free-tier queue times during peak hours test your patience precisely when inspiration strikes.

## Where It Sits In A 2026 Stack

The pragmatic setup for an AI-video creator: Hailuo for character motion shots, Veo or Runway for cinematic sequences, Kling for long takes, and a still-image model upstream for consistent subjects. Hailuo's aggressive model-iteration cadence - new versions shipping every few months - means the gap rankings above should be checked monthly; the video race is the fastest-moving category on this entire site, and today's weakness can be next quarter's headline feature.
